claims.statement: An MCP config is a JSON document with a top-level `mcpServers` mapping of server name to a server definition; the repository's own `.mcp.json` declares two remote HTTP servers, `docs-langchain` and `reference-langchain`, each with `type: http` and a `url`.

MCP server entries accept both stdio (`command`/`args`/`env`) and remote (`url`/`headers`) transports declared via a `type` or `transport` key of `stdio`, `http`, or `sse`, and a remote server may opt into OAuth login with `auth: oauth`.
The `streamable_http` and `streamable-http` transport names from the MCP spec normalize to the app's canonical `http` transport so configs copy-pasted from upstream docs validate.

`resolve_mcp_server_env` expands `${VAR}` and `${VAR:-default}` references only in the `command`, `url`, `args`, `env`, and `headers` fields, copies every other field verbatim, and does not mutate the input.

Environment interpolation uses POSIX `:-` semantics: `${VAR:-default}` falls back to `default` when the variable is unset or empty, an unset `${VAR}` with no default is a hard error, and a malformed `${...}` reference is rejected rather than silently emitted so a typo cannot inject a garbage value into a URL, command, or header.

`discover_mcp_config_sources` probes three locations in ascending precedence — the user-level profile `.mcp.json`, `<project-root>/.deepagents/.mcp.json`, then `<project-root>/.mcp.json` — and tags each discovered path with an immutable `MCPConfigScope` (USER or PROJECT) rather than re-deriving trust from path shape.

When a user-scope config path collides with a project path (e.g. a relocated home equal to the repo root), the collision resolves toward project provenance so relocating the profile never grants the repo's own MCP file user-level trust.

`resolve_and_load_mcp_tools` is the single entry point that discovers, merges, trust-filters, disable-filters, validates, and loads MCP configs, layering user configs, plugin `additional_configs`, trusted project configs, and finally an `explicit_config_path` (highest precedence, with fatal parse errors), and returns immediately when `no_mcp` is True.

Project MCP servers — both stdio and remote — are trust-gated before any connection is attempted, because an attacker-controlled `.mcp.json` could SSRF or exfiltrate `${VAR}` headers during the discovery preflight.

Whole-config project trust comes only from `trust_project_mcp=True`; `False` and `None` are treated identically as no whole-config trust, and project servers then load solely via the user's scoped approval policy.

The user-level allow/deny policy is sourced only from the user's own config (never the repo) so a committed `.mcp.json` cannot self-approve; denied servers are dropped even from a trusted config, and if the policy cannot be read the loader fails closed rather than honoring whole-config trust or bypassing a saved rejection.

Trust is resolved after precedence so that rejecting a higher-precedence server definition never reveals a stale approved definition beneath it; every server, even a malformed one, passes through the trust filter.

Installing a plugin is treated as the user's trust decision for its bundled servers, so `additional_configs` servers load without per-server approval, but the user-level deny policy still applies and an unreadable policy fails closed.
`_load_tools_from_config` captures per-server config, auth, and setup failures into the returned `MCPServerInfo` list rather than propagating them, so one bad server never hides the others.

Tool loading runs in two bounded-concurrency passes — preflight/connect then discover/convert — with results folded back in config order so `server_infos` is deterministic and tools are sorted by name regardless of which probe finishes first.

Preflight expands `${VAR}` references, runs a connectivity check (remote reachability probe, or a `shutil.which` executable check off the event loop for stdio), and builds the transport-specific connection before discovery opens a throwaway session to list tools.
When a server's config used environment interpolation, failure messages are redacted to avoid echoing a resolved secret, while plain configs keep full detail.
For stdio servers, `_MCPStderrSink` drains the subprocess stderr so a chatty server cannot block on a full pipe, and logs bounded, sanitized lines at DEBUG.
Runtime MCP tools bind in one of three ways: to a caller-owned session manager, to a new local session manager returned to the caller, or fully stateless (a fresh session per tool call).

`MCPSessionManager` caches one lazily created session per server and refuses to be reconfigured to a different connection signature once any session is active, preventing live sessions from being rebound to different transports or auth providers.
Each configured MCP server ends in one of the load states `ok`, `unauthenticated`, `awaiting_reconnect`, `error`, or `disabled`.

`MCPServerInfo.__post_init__` enforces a consistency invariant: an `ok` server carries no error, a non-`ok` server carries an error message and no tools, and `pending_reconnect` requires `status='disabled'`.

`MCPServerInfo.uses_oauth` is set only when a server's connection carries an OAuth provider (config opted in, or prior tokens exist with no overriding static Authorization header), so the TUI can offer re-authentication only where it is meaningful.

User-disabled server names persist under `[mcp].disabled_servers` in `~/.deepagents/config.toml`, are dropped at config merge time so no connection is attempted and no tools reach the agent, and are still surfaced as `disabled` `MCPServerInfo` entries so the user can re-enable them.
If a managed (administrator) MCP deny list is present but unreadable, the loader fails closed and disables every server rather than starting one an administrator may have blocked.
Discovered MCP tools are converted with `tool_name_prefix=True`, producing LangChain tool names of the form `{server_name}_{tool_name}`.
`server_graph` appends loaded MCP tools to the agent's other tools, loading them with `stateless=True` against a shared session manager.

MCP tools carry a `_deepagents_code_mcp` metadata marker; `auto_mode.is_mcp_tool` detects it, and in Auto mode `_deterministic_allow` auto-approves an MCP tool call only when it is coherently read-only, otherwise requiring review.
`mcp_tool_is_coherently_read_only` returns True only when the MCP tool's `readOnlyHint` metadata is literally `true`, `destructiveHint` is not `true`, and every present hint value is a real boolean.

A remote MCP server gets an OAuth provider when the config opted in with `auth: oauth` or a prior login stored tokens without an overriding static Authorization header (static headers take precedence), and a server that opted into OAuth with no stored tokens is skipped as `unauthenticated` requiring upfront login.

`FileTokenStorage` persists OAuth tokens per server under the profile's `mcp-tokens` state directory, keyed by a stem combining the path-safe server name and a hash of the resolved server URL, and writes an absolute expiry sidecar so a cold-started provider can trigger a refresh grant instead of a full browser re-auth.

A cross-process file lock serializes MCP token refreshes and a safety margin refreshes access tokens ahead of their advertised expiry to absorb clock skew, avoiding an unnecessary full browser re-auth.

`build_oauth_provider` uses a loopback callback server when the provider policy supports one (reusing a prior DCR port so the registered redirect_uri stays valid) or a paste-back handler otherwise, and installs re-auth-required handlers instead of prompting when non-interactive.

`login` (invoked as `dcode mcp login <server>`) drives the full OAuth handshake for an http/sse server, resolving env vars, running the provider policy's login (loopback, paste-back, or RFC 8628 device flow), and persisting tokens on success.

During discovery a token-refresh failure is classified `unauthenticated`, and a remote 401 OAuth challenge (RFC 9728) on a server not opted into OAuth is also surfaced as `unauthenticated` with a `dcode mcp login` hint rather than an opaque connection error.
MCP OAuth code never logs token material, passing only structural facts, and it filters out the SDK's expected re-auth log records because the app replaces them with an actionable hint.

`mcp_oauth_ui.OAuthInteraction` is a UI-agnostic protocol (authorize URL display, paste-back callback, device-code instructions, success/failure) implemented by both the CLI and TUI, and implementations must never embed token material in user-facing messages.

`mcp_login_service` extracts login-target config discovery, trust gating, and shape validation into pure functions returning structured results (`ConfigResolution`, `ServerSelection`, and a typed `ConfigResolutionError`) so both the CLI and TUI can render the outcome without relying on `print`.

Talon reuses the `deepagents_code.mcp_tools` loader: `load_mcp_tools` calls `resolve_and_load_mcp_tools` with an `explicit_config_path` from the first of `DEEPAGENTS_TALON_MCP_CONFIG`/`MCP_CONFIG`, a `ProjectContext` from `DEEPAGENTS_TALON_WORKSPACE`, `trust_project_mcp=None`, and wraps config errors in `MCPConfigError`, returning an `MCPTools` record of tools and per-server statuses.

Talon reuses the shared discovery order: `discover_mcp_config_paths` returns existing config files lowest-to-highest and `print_mcp_config_paths` renders `MCP_CONFIG_DISCOVERY_PATHS` (including `~/.deepagents/.mcp.json` and the two project locations) with found/missing markers.
